analysis.one_liner: Tightens safety, security, and evacuation requirements for nuclear power plant licenses.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have tightened safety, security, and evacuation requirements for nuclear plant licenses, never received a hearing or a vote and died in committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it harder to keep old nuclear plants running. It required that any nuclear plant — new or up for license renewal — not pose an unreasonable safety or security risk, including from terrorist attacks, and that emergency evacuation plans covering people within 50 miles be approved by federal agencies and nearby states. License renewals would have had to meet the same standards as a brand-new plant, and if surrounding population growth made a site unsuitable for a new plant, that could block renewal. The bill never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People living near nuclear plants — many of them clustered around aging reactors like Indian Point in the sponsor's district — would gain stronger legal protection: licenses could not be issued or renewed without proven evacuation plans and a finding that the plant does not pose an unreasonable safety or security threat, including from terrorism.

how_it_helps.text: It required the Nuclear Regulatory Commission to find that a licensed plant does not pose an unreasonable threat to people or the environment, including vulnerability to terrorist attacks, before issuing or renewing a license.

It required federal- and state-approved evacuation plans covering everyone within 50 miles of a plant, and made license renewals meet the same strict standards as brand-new plants, accounting for population growth around aging sites.

analysis.who_pays: Nuclear plant owners and operators, who would bear the cost of meeting stricter licensing and renewal standards and, in some cases, might have plants unable to relicense — costs that could partly pass to electricity customers.

drawbacks.text: Requiring license renewals to meet the same standards as brand-new construction could effectively force the shutdown of existing nuclear plants, which supply roughly a fifth of U.S. electricity and produce no carbon emissions.
The 50-mile evacuation-approval requirement would give states far from a plant veto power over its operation, which utilities argued could be unworkable.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addressed a real gap: nuclear licenses were renewed without checking whether evacuation plans still worked for a grown population or whether plants could withstand terrorist attack. Costs fall on plant owners, who would face tougher relicensing; some argue stricter renewal criteria could shorten plant lives and raise electricity prices. It was never debated, so neither the benefits nor those costs were ever weighed publicly.

outcome.mechanism: The House Energy and Commerce Committee referred it to a subcommittee in April 2009 and nothing ever came of it; the bill expired when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce on April 2, 2009, the day it was introduced.
Three weeks later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Environment, where it stayed with no further action.
It never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nuclear plant operators benefit, since the stricter safety, security, and evacuation standards were never imposed on them.

for.name: Rep. Nita Lowey
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to require stronger safety, security, and evacuation standards for nuclear plant licenses.

for.name: Reps. John Hall and Maurice Hinchey
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill after receiving the referral.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Democrats ever supported the bill and no Republican action is recorded; the bill died in committee without a vote, so no party-line positions were ever revealed.

industries.note: License renewals would no longer be near-automatic: plants would have to prove modern safety and security standards and state-approved evacuation plans, and population growth could force a plant out. Residents near plants would gain protection.
